summary: Minor children, disabled children, a disabled spouse, parents and dependants are guaranteed at least half of what they would inherit by law, whatever the will says. The sources do not settle whether a foreign resident can choose their own national law. Armenia has no common-law trust and the Hague Trusts Convention is not in force there; foundations exist but are set up for public-benefit purposes.
reserved_share: Minor and disabled children, disabled spouse and parents, and dependants: at least one half of the share they would take on intestacy, regardless of the will (Civil Code art. 1194, as quoted by Armenian legal sources).
foreign_law_note: I did not find the text of Armenia's conflict rule for succession or any rule allowing a foreign resident to choose their national law. Foreign-made wills are recognised as to form if they meet the law of the place they were made and are apostilled or legalised.
trust_note: Armenia is not on the HCCH status table for the 1985 Trusts Convention. I found no trust statute; the Civil Code is believed to provide only a contract of trust management of property (Russian-model), not a common-law trust. Foundations are governed by a Law on Foundations (2002) and are aimed at non-profit, public-benefit purposes; I could not confirm whether a purely private family foundation is allowed.
open_questions: Confirm the text of Civil Code art. 1194 (reserved share) and any conflict-of-laws article for succession from the official Armenian legal database.
Confirm whether the Civil Code's trust-management contract and the 2002 Law on Foundations allow any family-benefit use.
